newsitem.title: BRAZIL: BRAZIL STOCK FUNDS SEEN DRAWING LOWER INFLOWS.
newsitem.headline: BRAZIL STOCK FUNDS SEEN DRAWING LOWER INFLOWS.

text.p: The flow of cash into Brazilian equity funds will moderate in coming months as domestic investors adopt a more guarded position after the bolsa's extreme volatility in July, asset managers said.

"The money will keep coming in, but the flow of cash will no longer be as high as it was in the first half," said Marcelo Giufrida, asset manager at Credit Commerciale de France's Banco CCF do Brasil and director at Brazil's National Association of Investment Bankers (ANBID).
"The volatility scared away investors," he added.
A surprising 9.1 billion reais entered the local funds in the first six months of the year, contributing to the bolsa's exceptional gains of over 70 percent in the period.
The flood of money into the funds reached its peak in May and June, when a number of retail investors were drawn by the stock market's high returns.
But the massive cash inflows were interrupted when the bolsa tumbled in a frenetic profit-taking jag triggered by fears of a devaluation in Brazil's real currency.
The wind-shear on the bolsa caused an exodus from the funds, which hit its worst point July 15, with outflows at 500 million reais for the day.
Despite the large withdrawals, latest banking sector data showed that the funds still managed to end July with a net inflow of 1.409 billion reais.
Analysts said, however, the July data was somewhat distorted by money that came into so-called free portfolio funds whose assets are highly invested in derivatives like stock options.
"Those funds have a characteristic of a short-term fixed-income investment rather than equity," an asset manager said.
Banking sector statistics also showed that combined stock fund assets in July grew 9.17 percent to 19.4 billion reais, now accounting for 14 percent of the Brazilian fund industry's total assets.
Although flows into the funds are seen moderate by year end, asset managers do not believe individuals will abandon Brazilian shares for good.
"Those investors will now invest in stocks with a long-term perspective. They will be more patient to wait (to see the returns)," said CCF's Giufrida.
Analysts also said stock funds should continue attracting retail investors as fixed-income yields have dropped sharply due to the government's interest rate-cutting efforts.
